# High-Performance and Distributed Computing {#sec-hpc}

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Choose between `parallel`, `future`, `furrr`, and
  `mirai`/`crew` for a given parallelization problem and
  explain the cost model that governs the choice.
- Distinguish embarrassingly parallel work from work with
  inter-process communication, and recognize when the
  overhead of parallelism exceeds its benefit.
- Use Apache Arrow and `arrow` for out-of-memory tabular
  data, and DuckDB for SQL-style analytics on data larger
  than RAM.
- Decide when to move work to a GPU via `torch`, and
  recognize the small set of statistical workloads where
  GPU acceleration actually pays off.
- Reason about cloud computation (instance selection,
  spot/preemptible pricing, storage tiers) in terms of
  total cost of ownership rather than just hourly rate.
- Profile and benchmark before parallelizing; document the
  intended speedup and confirm it on representative data.

## Orientation

Statistical computation often runs on a single laptop
until, at some point, it cannot. A bootstrap with 1000
replicates finishes in ten minutes, but the same bootstrap
on the production cohort with hundreds of strata stalls
overnight. A posterior predictive check that ran without
difficulty on a 5% sample crashes the R session at full
sample. A Monte Carlo study that completed in an afternoon
now needs a week of runs.

In this chapter we shall cover the next layer above the
laptop. Most statistical work is **embarrassingly
parallel** (independent replicates of the same
computation), and the right tool for that case is rarely
the most sophisticated one. We begin with the parallelism
stack in R. We then work through out-of-memory tabular
data with Arrow and DuckDB, touch on GPU computation where
it matters, and end with cloud-cost reasoning.

The framing throughout is to **profile before
parallelizing, parallelize the right loop, and verify that
the speedup is real.** Parallelization is one of the few
engineering moves that can both speed work up and silently
corrupt results, and we treat it accordingly.

## The statistician's contribution {#sec-hpc-human}

GPUs and clusters solve compute problems. The
statistician's role is to ensure that the compute problem
being solved is the right one, and that the speedup is
bought at a cost the project can afford.

**(Judgment 1.) Parallelize the right level.** A naive
intuition is to parallelize the innermost loop.
Unfortunately, this is almost always wrong. The right
level is the *outermost* embarrassingly parallel loop: the
bootstrap replicate, the simulation iteration, the
cross-validation fold. Parallel overhead (process startup,
data serialization, and result collection) is paid once
per dispatched task. Splitting a fast inner loop across
workers can therefore leave us slower than the serial
version. The statistician identifies the right unit of
parallelism by understanding where the natural
independence lies. An LLM that says 'use `mclapply`' has
elided the question.

**(Judgment 2.) Random-number reproducibility is a
correctness issue.** Two parallel workers using the same
seed will produce identical 'random' replicates. For a
Monte Carlo study this is catastrophic, and it fails
silently. That is, the run completes, the output looks
reasonable, and the variance estimate is wrong. The
defense is L'Ecuyer's parallel RNG
(`set.seed(., kind = "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")` plus per-task seed
advancement)
or the `future` framework's `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)`.
The statistician must specify reproducibility requirements
before parallelizing, since LLMs frequently produce
parallel code that is fast but wrong on RNG.

**(Judgment 3.) Cloud cost is your problem.** Spot
instances are 60 to 90% cheaper than on-demand, but they
can be reclaimed mid-run. Consider a 12-hour Stan fit on a
spot instance that is reclaimed at hour 11. It has cost
the spot rate for 11 hours and produced no output. The
statistician decides whether to use spot, on-demand, or
reserved instances. The decision rests on the value of a
partial completion, the cost of a restart, and the
deadline. These are project-management choices, and an
unplanned cloud bill can exhaust a project budget.

## The R parallelism stack

Four frameworks cover most R parallel workloads.

**`parallel` (base R).** `mclapply()` (forking, Unix only)
and `parLapply()` (PSOCK clusters, cross-platform) are the
oldest tools. They work and are well understood. However,
they are also the most error-prone interface, particularly
around RNG seeds, error propagation, and progress
reporting. We use them when no dependency on `future` is
acceptable.

**`future` and `furrr`.** `future` [@bengtsson2021unifying]
provides a uniform API for asynchronous computation across
backends: sequential, multicore, multisession, cluster,
and cloud. `furrr::future_map()` is the parallel
counterpart of `purrr::map()`, and it handles RNG
correctly with `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)`. This is the
recommended default for applied parallelism. Code written
with `future_map()` runs on a laptop, a workstation, or a
cluster with one `plan()` call.

**`mirai` and `crew`.** `mirai` is a lighter,
lower-overhead alternative to `future` for high-throughput
dispatch. `crew` builds on `mirai` to support persistent
workers and auto-scaling, and it is the engine behind the
parallelism in `targets`. For pipelines that dispatch many
short tasks, `crew` is substantially more efficient than
`future`, with seconds rather than minutes of overhead at
scale.

**`batchtools`.** For HPC clusters with schedulers (SLURM,
PBS, LSF), `batchtools` is the established interface. On
the one hand, it has a steeper learning curve and is
overkill for laptop or workstation work. On the other, it
is the right tool when we need to submit thousands of jobs
to a scheduler and harvest the results.

A worked example contrasts the styles. To illustrate,
suppose we want to fit 500 bootstrap replicates of a
regression model.

````{.r}
library(furrr)
plan(multisession, workers = 8)

boot_fit <- function(i, data) {
  resample <- data[sample(nrow(data), replace = TRUE), ]
  coef(lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = resample))
}

results <- future_map(
  1:500,
  ~boot_fit(.x, my_data),
  .options = furrr_options(seed = TRUE)
)
````

The `.options = furrr_options(seed = TRUE)` argument is
non-negotiable. Without it, `future_map` will warn but
proceed, and the resulting 'replicates' may not be
statistically independent.

**The cost model**, simplified, is as follows:

- Forking (`mclapply` on Unix) shares memory copy-on-write;
  startup cost is microseconds.
- PSOCK clusters and `multisession` workers spawn fresh R
  sessions; startup cost is seconds and memory must be
  serialized across the boundary.
- Cluster backends pay scheduler queueing time on top.

The implication is as follows. If the task is sub-second
and copy-on-write is available, we fork. If the task takes
seconds to minutes and we need cross-platform support, we
use `multisession`. If the task takes minutes to hours and
we have scheduler access, we batch.

## Out-of-memory tabular data: Arrow and DuckDB

When a dataset will not fit in RAM, the right move is
rarely 'rent a bigger machine.' Instead, we switch to
columnar out-of-memory tools that read only the columns
and rows required.

**Apache Arrow** is a columnar in-memory format and a set
of tools for working with it. The R `arrow` package binds
to the C++ implementation. A typical query is as follows:

````{.r}
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

ds <- open_dataset("data/large_cohort/", format = "parquet")
ds |>
  filter(year == 2024, site %in% c("A","B")) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
````

The query is built lazily, and no data are read until
`collect()` materializes the result into an in-memory
tibble. Arrow pushes the filter down to the file scan, so
only the rows matching the predicate are decoded. On a
50 GB Parquet dataset this can be the difference between
two seconds and two hours.

**DuckDB** [@raasveldt2019duckdb] is an embedded
analytical database, similar to SQLite but
column-oriented and tuned for OLAP queries. The `duckdb`
and `duckplyr` R packages expose DuckDB through a
`dplyr`-compatible interface. DuckDB excels at SQL-shaped
analytics on data larger than RAM, at joins, and at window
functions. For a project that already works in SQL, DuckDB
is often the cleanest path.

````{.r}
library(duckdb); library(DBI); library(dplyr)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "CREATE VIEW cohort AS
  SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/large_cohort/*.parquet')")
tbl(con, "cohort") |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  count(site) |>
  collect()
````

The decision between Arrow and DuckDB is largely about
ergonomics. Arrow integrates more naturally with `dplyr`
pipelines and the broader R ecosystem. DuckDB is faster on
complex joins and excels at SQL-shaped work. Many projects
use both, with Arrow to read and filter and DuckDB to
join.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: when not to parallelize

**Question.** A colleague has a `purrr::map()` call over 10
elements, each taking about 50 ms. They propose switching to
`furrr::future_map()` to speed it up. Should they?

**Answer.**

No. The total serial time is about 500 ms. Spawning a
multisession `future` plan typically costs more than a
second per worker for R session startup, plus
serialization overhead per task. The parallel version will
therefore be slower than the serial version.
Parallelization is profitable when total serial time
substantially exceeds parallel overhead, and sub-second
loops over a handful of items are below that threshold. We
would run the serial version, profile it, and parallelize
only the loops that dominate.

:::

## GPU computation: where it matters and where it does not

GPUs accelerate dense linear algebra and matrix-shaped
computation. Most statistical workloads are not
matrix-shaped in the way GPUs reward. As a result, most
attempts to move statistical code to a GPU end up slower
or no faster. The narrow class of problems in which a GPU
pays off is as follows:

- **Deep learning and neural network training.** `torch`
  for R and `tensorflow`/`keras` are the established
  interfaces. These are GPU-native and benefit from
  order-of-magnitude speedups on appropriately sized
  models.
- **Large dense matrix algebra.** Models that hinge on
  Cholesky or eigendecomposition of dense matrices in the
  thousands-of-rows range can benefit from GPU BLAS. The
  OpenCL-based `gpuR` package that once exposed this was
  archived from CRAN in November 2025; `torch` tensors
  now provide GPU linear algebra from R.
- **Stan and PyMC under specific configurations.** Stan
  can run gradient evaluations on a GPU for some model
  classes, and PyMC via JAX/NumPyro can target GPU and
  TPU. Speedups are model-dependent, so we benchmark
  before assuming any benefit.

What does *not* benefit from a GPU? The list includes
looping over heterogeneous small models, data
manipulation, most regression fitting on small-to-medium
datasets, and any workload bottlenecked by data movement
to and from GPU memory. The CPU↔GPU memory transfer is
often the dominant cost. If the inner loop touches GPU
memory many times, the gain is lost.

The decision rule is empirical. We benchmark a
representative sub-problem on CPU and GPU before
committing infrastructure to a GPU-based pipeline.

## Cloud computation and cost discipline

Three observations dominate cloud-cost reasoning for
statistics.

**Spot instances are 60 to 90% cheaper but reclaimable.**
AWS spot, Azure low-priority, and GCP preemptible
instances offer substantial discounts. In exchange, the
provider retains the right to reclaim them on short
notice. For fault-tolerant workloads, such as a Monte
Carlo study in which individual replicates can be retried,
they are excellent. For long-running serial fits with no
checkpointing, they are dangerous. We either save state at
every iteration (so that a reclaim is at most a small
loss) or pay for on-demand.

**Storage tiers compound.** S3 standard storage is roughly
3 to 4× cheaper per GB-month than general-purpose EBS
volumes attached to a running instance. Holding 50 TB of
intermediate data on EBS for a six-month project is
therefore materially more expensive than holding it on S3
with on-demand access. The pattern that scales is to keep
cold data on S3, mount only the working subset to compute,
and write results back to S3. `arrow::s3_bucket()` and
`arrow::open_dataset()` make this idiomatic from R.

**Right-size, do not over-size.** The instance type with
the most cores is rarely the right answer for a
statistical workload. Memory-bandwidth-bound work (most R)
benefits more from fewer fast cores with high memory
bandwidth than from many slow cores. Compute-bound matrix
work may benefit from the opposite. We run a benchmark on
a small instance, project the runtime to a large one, and
pick the smallest instance that meets the deadline.

**Infrastructure as code** manages this complexity. Tools
such as `paws` and `googleCloudStorageR` script
provisioning, and `targets` with cloud-aware backends
dispatches and harvests work. In this pattern, a
`_targets.R` pipeline runs locally on a laptop and on a
cluster with the same code. It is parametrized only by the
`crew` controller it uses.

## Worked example: a parallel bootstrap with reproducible RNG

To illustrate, consider a 5000-replicate bootstrap of a
Cox proportional hazards model fit. The example uses
explicit RNG handling and a `targets` pipeline that scales
from laptop to cluster.

````{.r}
# _targets.R
library(targets)
library(crew)

tar_option_set(
  packages = c("survival", "dplyr"),
  controller = crew_controller_local(workers = 8)
)

boot_one <- function(i, data) {
  ix <- sample(nrow(data), replace = TRUE)
  fit <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ trt + age + stage,
               data = data[ix, ])
  coef(fit)
}

list(
  tar_target(cohort, readRDS("data/cohort.rds")),
  tar_target(boot_index, seq_len(5000)),
  tar_target(
    boot_replicates,
    boot_one(boot_index, cohort),
    pattern = map(boot_index),
    iteration = "list",
    cue = tar_cue(seed = TRUE)
  ),
  tar_target(
    boot_summary,
    do.call(rbind, boot_replicates) |>
      apply(2, function(x) c(
        est = mean(x), lo = quantile(x, 0.025),
        hi = quantile(x, 0.975)
      ))
  )
)
````

`crew_controller_local(workers = 8)` runs locally.
Swapping to `crew.cluster::crew_controller_slurm()` reuses
the same pipeline on a SLURM cluster with one line
changed. `targets` derives each target's seed
deterministically from the global seed option and the
target's name, so rerunning the same pipeline produces the
same bootstrap distribution. The cue
`cue = tar_cue(seed = TRUE)` controls whether a target
reruns when its seed changes.

For comparison, a serial benchmark gives the following:

````{.r}
serial <- system.time({
  out <- lapply(1:500, boot_one, data = cohort)
})
# user.self  sys.self   elapsed
#   42.13     0.51       42.78
````

With 8 workers under `crew`, the same 500 replicates take
about 7.4 seconds, a speedup of 5.8× after serialization
and dispatch overhead. The full 5000-replicate run
completes in just over a minute. The same pipeline
deployed to a 64-worker cluster runs in under 10 seconds.

## Collaborating with an LLM on HPC

LLMs are useful for translating serial R code to a
parallel form, for suggesting Arrow and DuckDB query
rewrites, and for reasoning about cloud cost trade-offs.
They are unreliable on parallel RNG and on diagnosing why
a parallel run is slower than serial. They are also
unreliable on GPU benchmarking, where their advice tends
toward blanket optimism.

**Prompt 1: 'Parallelize this bootstrap loop with reproducible
RNG.'** Provide the serial loop. Ask for a `future_map`
version with proper seed handling.

*What to watch for.* The LLM may produce parallel code
without `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)`. It may instead call
`set.seed()` inside the worker, which is a correctness bug
because it produces identical replicates across workers.
It may also suggest `mclapply()` without the
`mc.set.seed = TRUE` argument and the
`RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")` setup that makes it work.

*Verification.* Run the parallel version twice with the
same seed; the bootstrap distribution should be identical.
Then run it once and inspect a small number of replicates
for duplicate values across workers. Identical replicates
from different worker indices are a definitive signature
of an RNG bug.

**Prompt 2: 'Why is my parallel run slower than serial?'**
Paste the serial timing, the parallel timing, the worker
count, the per-iteration work, and the data size.

*What to watch for.* The LLM will often suggest 'increase
workers' or 'switch backends' without diagnosing the
underlying issue. The common causes are too-fine-grained
parallelism, large per-task data serialization, and thread
oversubscription in BLAS-using code. Diagnosing them
requires the LLM to ask clarifying questions about
per-task work size and data movement. If the LLM does not
ask, push back.

*Verification.* Profile a single worker iteration with
`profvis`. Compute the total work time, the parallel
overhead per task, and the projected speedup with $W$
workers. If the projected speedup is less than 2×,
parallelization is not the right intervention, and the
loop should be restructured instead.

**Prompt 3: 'Should I use spot or on-demand instances for
this 8-hour Stan fit?'** Provide the workload, deadline, and
checkpointing capability.

*What to watch for.* The LLM defaults to recommending spot
for cost reasons. It typically does not weigh the cost of
a mid-run reclaim. For an 8-hour fit with no
checkpointing, a reclaim at hour 7 wastes the full
instance cost and the elapsed time before a re-run. The
right answer depends on the tolerance for re-runs and on
the deadline.

*Verification.* If the model can checkpoint (save Stan's
warm-up state, resume), spot is fine. If it cannot,
compute the expected cost, including the probability of
reclaim times the redo cost. To illustrate, a 5% reclaim
probability on an 8-hour fit means an expected 24 minutes
of waste per run. On a \$10/hour instance that is \$4 of
expected waste against roughly \$48 in savings. Spot still
wins, but the calculation should be made.

In practice, we use LLMs for code translation and do the
cost and correctness reasoning ourselves. They are
competent on the syntactic mechanics of parallelism (which
package, which function). They are weak on the
operational questions of whether the result will actually
be faster, be correct, or cost less.

## Principle in use

Three habits define defensible HPC work:

1. **Profile first, parallelize second.** A serial run with
   `profvis` identifies the bottleneck. Parallelizing a
   non-bottleneck wastes engineering time and adds bugs.
   The 80/20 rule applies: most of the runtime is in 20%
   of the code, and that 20% is what we parallelize.

2. **Make RNG explicit and tested.** Every parallel
   computation that uses random numbers must specify
   `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)` or its equivalent. We test
   by running the pipeline twice with the same seed, and
   the results must match exactly. If they do not, the
   pipeline has a correctness bug.

3. **Cost-budget the run.** Before submitting a long cloud
   job, write down the expected runtime, the per-hour cost,
   the total budget, and the kill criterion. A \$400/day
   instance left running over a forgotten weekend has cost
   real projects real money. Set up billing alerts, and
   check them.

## Exercises

1. Take a serial Monte Carlo study of your choice (1000
   replicates, each ~1 second). Implement it three ways:
   `mclapply`, `furrr::future_map` with multisession, and
   `crew` via `targets`. Benchmark each. Account for the
   overhead difference; does the cheapest framework give
   the lowest total time on this workload?

2. Convert a `dplyr` pipeline that operates on a 5 GB CSV
   to operate on a Parquet dataset via Arrow. Measure the
   speedup on (a) a column-subsetting query, (b) a `filter`
   + `summarize` query, and (c) a self-join. Identify which
   query benefits most from columnar layout and explain
   why.

3. Set up a SLURM (or PBS) job submission for a 100-replicate
   simulation using `targets` with `crew.cluster`. Configure
   it to run on the cluster but also to run locally with no
   code change. Document the configuration switch.

4. Profile a `brms` fit with `profvis`. Identify the three
   most expensive steps. Are any of them parallelizable
   without modifying Stan? (Hint: most are not.)

5. Cost-model a 200-iteration MCMC study where each chain
   takes 4 hours. Assume an on-demand `c5.4xlarge` is
   \$0.68/hour, spot is \$0.20/hour, and spot reclaim
   probability is 8%. With 200 chains needed and four
   chains per instance, compute the total expected cost
   under each strategy. Document your assumptions.

## Further reading

- @bengtsson2021unifying, *A Unifying Framework for
  Parallel and Distributed Processing in R using Futures*.
  The reference for the `future` ecosystem.
- @raasveldt2019duckdb, *DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical
  Database*. The original DuckDB paper.
- The Apache Arrow project documentation for R
  (<https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/>) is current and
  comprehensive.
- The `targets` user manual
  (<https://books.ropensci.org/targets/>) is the canonical
  reference for reproducible pipelines, with extensive HPC
  backend coverage.
